text: Last weekend, Houthis attacked Riyadh airport in a dramatic escalation. This was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. And in response, Saudi Arabia has had to close the airport and it's also cancelled several major international events that it was scheduled to host this week. So how did we get to this point? What options does Saudi Arabia have going forward?

What would a major escalation in the war look like? Or what could a deal with the Houthis look like? And is there a role for the United States? Today on State of Play, we're asking, after Houthi attacks, what options does Saudi Arabia have? Okay, I often say that we have the perfectly placed guests to talk about this topic, but I think it is more true today than it has been. In many of our episodes, I'm really delighted to have returning to State of Play, I think

maybe for the third time, Michael, Ambassador Michael Ratney, who is both a non-resident senior advisor in the Middle East program here at CSIS, and also was most recently the U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia until, when was it, until early 2025? At the beginning of last year, yeah. Yeah, exactly. And Michael, you were just in Saudi Arabia last week, right? Last week, yeah. Okay, okay. I'm really looking forward to what you heard.

And then I'm absolutely delighted to welcome our newest colleague in CSIS, Alison Miner, who is a senior fellow in the Middle East program. And Alison was previously the Deputy Special Envoy to Yemen, and also Director of Arabian Affairs on the National Security Council in the White House. Alison, welcome to CSIS. Welcome to State of Play. Thank you very much. So you've been here for all of three days, I think, so far.

You've already put out a commentary, and we'll link to that in the show notes and also a video. I hope you're settling in okay so far, although I know you're hitting the ground running. No, it's really great to be here at CSIS, but of course, the situation in the Middle East doesn't let us have a slow on-ramp, so really, really happy to contribute. Firstly, for our audience who don't know, who haven't been following Yemen and Saudi Arabia as closely, can you give us a sense of sort of how we got to this point?

So why are the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia at the moment? And maybe, Alison, actually, should I start with you on this? So the current situation really stretches back to 2014, when the Houthis seized control of Sana'a with the help of the former president of Yemen, and in doing so, disrupted what was a peaceful political transition process coming off of Yemen's Arab Spring. So after the Houthis seized control of the capital and pushed further into the country,

Saudi Arabia launched a campaign with other members of the coalition to try to restore the Yemen government. That campaign really started to stalemate around 2018, 2019, and we saw the front lines stay relatively static since that point. And there were a series of political processes to try to resolve this conflict, but ultimately, they kept getting derailed for a number of reasons. There was success in 2022, a UN-sponsored truce took hold, and while it was technically

expired in October 2022, a de facto truce took hold. So the war in Yemen was not settled, but there was a relative calm that took place. But unfortunately, because the conflict itself, the political questions at the heart of the conflict were not resolved, it seemed that an escalation was inevitable. And I have to say, it was really the Houthi Red Sea campaign in 2023 that derailed efforts to try to secure that more durable resolution.

And I think, you know, since... Yeah, and that campaign, the Houthis began to threaten shipping going through the Red Sea. They said this was in support of Palestinians in the aftermath of the October 7th attacks, and then of course, Israel's operations in Gaza. And that was kind of a bit of a prelude to what we saw then, maybe with Iran threatening ships going through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. Yeah, I think that's a really important point.

Essentially, what the Houthis did with the Bab el-Mendeb in 2023 and 2024 was demonstrate that you can close or constrain a maritime strait without actually having to physically close it. Basically, you just drive up the commercial risk and make it untenable for most actors to continue to use that waterway. And so that's something that we saw Iran replicate with the Strait of Hormuz, you know, just a year or two later. Michael, how has Saudi Arabia's thinking about Yemen, a very big picture, shifted in recent years, would you say?

So the simplest way of thinking about it is they've really shifted early on from this sense that the Houthis were this tribal insurgency that they should be able to dispatch with ease to realizing that it was a morass dealing with them, even with significant U.S. support after 2014 and 2015. And so they went from escalation, ultimately unsatisfactory. The Houthis were intact, although there were large numbers of civilian casualties that kind of drove international perception to an effort to deescalate, reach a truce, as

Alison said, maintain that kind of uneasy truce. Really, until quite recently, until the last couple of months when the Houthis, for a variety of reasons, kind of got into the fight that started effectively with the Iran war at the end of February and the Houthis fully into it in a way that was highly antagonistic towards the Saudis. And the Saudis are back now, not just attacking military or energy targets, but, you know, trying to murder civilians at the airport in Riyadh, for example.

The Houthis fully into it and the Saudis back to this sense of this time we're serious once and for all, we have to get rid of these guys. And as I mentioned, you were just in Saudi Arabia last week while these attacks happened, or did you leave before the attacks? So I got there the day before. So the day after I got there, there was this first attack at the airport that we think was intercepted. There was definitely a loud boom and we were there the full week and we were going to

leave Friday. We ended up leaving via Manama instead of Riyadh just to avoid the airport. And then the next day on Saturday was that really horrific attack in which, you know, multiple deaths, many, many injured people. And from there, you know, it's just become in a sense of major escalation on the part of the Houthis. And how would you say sort of Saudis are responding now? What's what's the what did you sense of the atmosphere in Saudi Arabia?

You know, Riyadh, it's interesting. And on the one hand, it feels very normal driving around, eating in restaurants like life goes on. Clearly, the Saudis want to project that sense of normality, but it's kind of also unnerving. And it's the Saudis in some way are used to the Houthis being their principal antagonist. But the idea that they're now attacking civilian targets on purpose, so not just energy infrastructure, not just military bases, but actually targeting airports, trying to kill civilians. It's somewhat unnerving.

It's for the Saudi officials. I would talk to it in a way. It's changed their psychology. Their view now is we we just we need to be done with the Houthis. No more de-escalation. No more truces. We need to follow this thing through. We cannot coexist with these folks. So I definitely want to come back to that and the thinking of the Saudis going forward. But, Alison, maybe I could ask you, I think there was maybe some surprise early on in the war with Iran that the Houthis didn't really get involved for for a while.

Why do you think the Houthis have chosen to attack or to escalate their attacks against Saudi Arabia at this point, what, seven, six, six, seven months into the into the war? Yeah, I think there are a lot of factors at play, but the first is a reminder that the Houthis are not simply going to get involved in this fight because Iran wants them to. Iran certainly has significant influence with the Houthis. They are culpable for the rapid expansion of Houthi capabilities over the past decade. But the Houthis have their own agenda, and at times they pursue that agenda more

aggressively than even Tehran might want them to. So I think Iran was encouraging the Houthis to get involved in the fight. Iran understands that because the Houthis can constrain traffic through the Bab el-Mendeb, they can create this double choke point crisis, staving off traffic through both the Hormuz and the Bab el-Mendeb. But for the Houthis, I think they saw, you know, the vulnerability that the conflict had created for Saudi Arabia, who then relied heavily on the Red Sea for their oil exports. And I think the Houthis were worried that, you know, should there be a deal between Saudi

Arabia and Iran or the U.S. and Iran, they might lose that window to exploit those Saudi vulnerabilities to ramp up their own demands for Riyadh. So I think that that was a factor at play. I think they also saw the support that Riyadh was funneling to the Yemen government, and they also anticipated that there could be a re-escalation of the conflict. And they understood that doing so, if they were to be able to trigger that escalation now while the Iran conflict is still hot, that they would be in a better position and the

Saudis would be more vulnerable. So I think there are a number of factors at play. And I do want to stress that Iran did have a hand in fanning the flames by sending in a Mohan air flight on July 13th that kind of staved off this or ticked off this this escalation. But they do not control what the Houthis are doing. OK, I would add it's it's kind of an odd situation where the Houthis are sort of less and less a proxy. That word, it applies in some sense, but less and less and oddly, almost perversely,

that's more dangerous. If they were a full on proxy, it meant you could cut a deal with the Iranians and it would impose itself on the Houthis. That's probably not true at this point. Yeah, I completely agree. And the Houthis ambitions, again, first and foremost, they need to cement their control inside of Yemen. But they have much grander ambitions. If you listen to what they say, it's about liberating Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem. That's a long term goal. But certainly in the medium term, they are expanding their control of the Red Sea. They are expanding their influence across the Horn of Africa, where they see these other

crises creating a ripe environment for them to exploit their own influence. So, again, I think we have to be mindful that the Houthis, they're not a proxy. They are worse. So it's not sounding like Saudi Arabia really has any easy options here because the Houthis are more independent. They have increased their capabilities. They're feeling emboldened, I think, right now and clearly have expanded their or they've gone up the escalation ladder very quickly. So, Michael, you began to say that Saudis that you spoke to seemed to be saying it's

not possible to go back to a truce now with the Houthis. They're too much of a threat. They need to be dealt with once and for all. What would that actually look like? It's a it's a terrible dilemma for the Saudis, because on the one hand, that is their view. And certainly as a political matter, as a national security matter, they can't not respond. They've been attacked on their own territory in a rather brazen way. On the other hand, they know full well that the Houthis have this ability to retaliate disproportionately, asymmetrically in ways that do significant damage to, you know, not

just civilian infrastructure, but the reputation of the country as a safe place for investors. So the Saudis can bomb military targets, rockets, drone production facilities in Yemen. The Houthis can retaliate in a way that in some ways is far more damaging. So it puts in front of the Saudis a horrible dilemma. I think it was a matter of practice. They're going to have to continue this effort to degrade the Houthis ability to launch these attacks. They want to get them off these positions that they took last month along

the Bab al-Mandab, this kind of strategic waterway. They're doing it with their partners, the Yemeni armed forces, the armed forces connected to the legitimate government of Yemen that are somewhat of a motley crew themselves, their collection of militias. They lack coherence. The Saudis are supporting them with airstrikes and advisers. But it's in some ways the Houthis are kind of more coherent, a fighting force, and it makes them devilishly difficult to confront.

Alison, you may have more views on this, but it means the Saudis, they have to pursue this. But my own take is eventually they have to find some kind of an off ramp. Yeah, Alison, what do you think? Yeah, I definitely agree with Michael that the Saudi attitude towards the Houthis has shifted significantly since we negotiated the truce in 2022 and we saw these talks between the Saudis and the Houthis over the course of 2023, where there's hope that there might be some path towards a very hesitant coexistence.

And I think their campaign in the Red Sea triggered that, their behavior over the past several months certainly just exacerbate that, and particularly the Riyadh airport attack. I think Saudi Arabia learned a lot of lessons over the course of the Yemen war from 2015 to 2022, and I do hope that they're learning some of those lessons about the consequences of pursuing a war without credible military objectives and past the point of the utility of continued offensive action.

And also the fact that there aren't quick and easy solutions to the challenges of their partner on the ground, the Yemen government. You know, I think the question here is, is now the time to deal with the Houthi threat for Riyadh, or is that something, you know, do they have to contain it for the time being and then seek to re-engage down the road when they've dealt with some of these real fundamental challenges, both within the Yemen government, but also within what was the

Saudi-led coalition, and most significantly, the relationship between Saudi Arabia and the UAE, who has in the past played a very significant role in ground offensives against the Houthis. And so when we talk about ground offensives, there were media reports that the Saudis were potentially turning to Syria to support with troops. And as far as I know, the Syrian president has not agreed to do that, at least not yet.

Is there a possibility that Saudi Arabia could launch a much more serious ground offensive in Yemen? Michael, is that, oh, sorry. Yeah, so I saw this, the Syria reports. It sounded like somebody, maybe the Syrians themselves had offered to support the Saudi effort against the Houthis. It was a little bit ambiguous to me, and it's awkward too, because obviously we're trying to get foreign forces out of Syria. It's a little odd to send foreign forces from Syria to another battlefront. So I don't know where that's going to go.

What the Saudis really want is support from the United States. What the Saudis really want is support from the United States, not from Syria. And it seems like they're getting some support from the U.S. Some reports I've said, I've seen suggest targeting assistance, intelligence sharing and so forth. They really want U.S. support on airstrikes against Houthi targets. OK, great. I wanted to talk about the U.S. role, because I think President Trump has said so far that he didn't want to get involved in Yemen. But then there have been several phone calls with MBS, with the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia.

So where do we see the role of the U.S. at this point? Are we expecting there to be greater support for airstrikes, as you said, Michael? Obviously, this is coming just weeks before the midterm elections here in the United States. So this is a time of greater sensitivity, perhaps domestically, for President Trump. Where do you see those calculations? I mean, at this point, it's hard to predict because of this highly personalized nature

of policymaking in Washington, right? It's one person's decision. Clearly, the Saudi leadership knows that and they've tried to influence that decision. And President Trump has sent mixed signals. On the one hand, he's sort of expressed solidarity with the Saudis, but he's not come out and suggested that we're going to up the degree of military support that we provide to them. And it may be, you know, we speculate here, but it may be a Pentagon issue. You know, U.S. forces following the whole campaign since the end of February are stretched

thin. Naval forces have been at sea for a long time or reportedly running out of the most sophisticated interceptors. So it may be military limitations or it may well be a political quandary that President Trump, who would love to see this war in the rearview mirror, doesn't want to open a new front that suggests that the war is not over. How that intersects with these, you know, the president has been teasing the idea of resuming the war against Iran after the midterms. I don't know how this question of whether or not there would be U.S. support for the

Saudis against the Houthis kind of jibes with the possibility of a resumed campaign against Iran. It's very, very muddled right now. And I think certainly for the Saudis and for the Yemeni government, it's frustrating because this is the moment where they want maximum clarity about what kind of support they can get. I would maybe just add to that. President Trump likes to support winners, and I simply don't think he sees the current campaign against the Houthis as a winner. And he has his own baggage from the U.S. airstrike campaign against the Houthis, which was

quite aggressive under President Trump, Operation Rough Rider, that was called off with a, you know, a rather hasty ceasefire in May 2025 without accomplishing its objective of stopping Houthi attacks against commercial shipping. So I think that that lingers in his mind as well. And there's another actor that I think is potentially willing to get involved in anti-Houthi operations, which is Israel. And Prime Minister Netanyahu has sort of talked about this. I think it's been floated as a way perhaps to advance or to accelerate efforts towards

normalization with Saudi Arabia. Michael, how would you assess the likelihood of Israel getting involved here? I think there's real reluctance by the Saudis to contemplate that. Now, the Israelis might have their own calculations and they might pursue attacks on the Houthis on their own. But I think the problem is that the Israelis, one of the main reasons the Israelis want to support Saudi efforts against the Houthis is to publicly talk about that support. So they can sort of suggest that there's Saudi-Israeli collaboration in a way that has a

political benefit for Israeli politicians. I think from the Saudi perspective, it's not worth it. Whatever kind of strategic benefit or even tactical benefit they get from Israeli efforts against the Houthis, I think is vitiated by the political problems that that creates for the Saudi leadership. The Israelis are exceedingly unpopular in Saudi Arabia right now and I don't know that Saudi support even against this common enemy would really resonate very well with the public there. There's another option could be to try to de-escalate and to try to come to some kind of agreement with the Houthis, at least for now, perhaps to buy time, to buy some calm. What do you think that could look like, Alison, and do you think this is actually a realistic option that the Saudis might be considering at this point? I am skeptical about the ability to de-escalate in the immediate term.

I think we're stuck in this escalatory spiral on both sides and it's going to be difficult to come down in the immediate term. But I do think, in my opinion, finding an off-ramp sooner rather than later is the best solution here. And I want to stress, you know, there's a lot of people, this is a very sensitive topic, especially for Yemenis who are sick of this sense of the international community pressuring them to basically cave into this group that is terrifying, you know, is deeply repressive, is violating Yemeni cultural and social norms, you know, just harassing the people under

their control and stoking this, you know, dire economic crisis in the country. But to me, it's not so much a question of caving to the Houthis. It's a question of giving space to provide a political alternative. You know, I really do think that the Houthis gain most of their strength from the weakness of their opponents. Most Yemenis just really do not believe that the Yemen government provides a credible alternative to Houthi rule. You know, it's deeply fragmented. And this is not just, you know, it's not just because they're, you know, a ragtag group

of militias. It's because the political visions of the groups that make up the Yemen government, this kind of loose coalition that they formed, are in some cases diametrically opposed. They have not been able to agree on a, you know, a credible unified political end state for Yemen. They were to liberate Sana'a, to decimate the Houthis, but they couldn't then lump the same type of uncertainty they did in 2014. Even then, it's not clear if Yemen would have a stable political resolution because of those

divisions within the Yemen government. So I really think, you know, the first step needs to be de-escalating the situation and trying to heal those rifts within the coalition and come up with that, that credible unified political vision for the country that you can then start rallying others around. Michael, do you see interest in Saudi Arabia to undertake or to try to support an initiative along those lines? I mean, if you ask them now, they're pretty sore, right? And I think they feel like the priority now is to degrade the Houthis, ideally vanquish

them completely. I think they know in their heart of hearts that they're going to have to return to some kind of a de-escalatory plan. In the past, that has been the two things the Houthis want, right? They want legitimacy, and in a sense, they got that from the Saudis through this roadmap, this direct political dialogue, and they want money, and the Saudis dangled the possibility of salary payments to government employees in Houthi areas that would have injected a lot of cash into the economy. I think the Saudis are loath to go down that road at least right now, and what Alison described

and you talk about this, Alison, in this essay that you just published is you also need a credible alternative to the Houthis, and I think the Saudis would certainly be supportive of that, but that is a longer-term proposition and takes a lot of, what do you want to say, a lot of patience, a lot of international support, but I don't think in the longer run there's an alternative, and I would add, I think in the longer run, we have to figure out a way to get rid of the Houthis, but we also have to figure out a way to empower some

kind of credible alternative that can govern the country decently or you're back to where you were. Yeah. If I can build on that quickly, because there's some in Washington who just say the Saudis should just give up, stop the war, tell the Houthis that they've won, and stop this mess, but what I think that neglects is the fact that what the Houthis are demanding is not simply a quick payoff or Saudi concessions economically. What the Houthis are asking for is to gain through negotiations what they have not been able to gain on the battlefield, and that is gaining control over Yemen's hydrocarbon

resources. Currently, they control most of the population, but none of those resources. It is cementing their control inside of Yemen, which are not ultimately things that Saudi Arabia can or should be able to give away. Currently, those resources are controlled by the Yemen government. The entirety of the south and some parts of the north are still controlled by groups affiliated with the Yemen government, and that control is existential for them. They will spoil if they think that the Saudis are going to start giving those things away. This was a dynamic a few years ago during negotiations, and it's still one today.

You cannot solve the Yemen conflict without having the Yemen government and the Houthis sitting across the table from each other. So far, the Houthis have been unwilling to do that. As we begin to wrap up, I want to ask you some rapid fire questions. My first one is to ask you to answer basically the title of the episode, so what options does Saudi Arabia have, but which option do you think is most likely in the short term? So something like more airstrikes, ground incursion, or some kind of agreement to de-escalate.

Michael, what do you see as most likely? So I think in the near term, there's going to be a significant Saudi escalation, more airstrikes, more military pressure, and messaging that the Saudi public needs to endure some of the retaliation that the Houthis undertake. But then beyond that, and not that far beyond that, I think we will see some kind of efforts to find an off-ramp. Maybe not a permanent off-ramp, but a near-term off-ramp.

I'm definitely worried about escalation right now. One thing I'm keeping an eye on in the past, in the pre-truce phase of the war, one thing that we saw the Saudi-led coalition and the Yemen government doing was trying to constrict the flow of goods through Hodeidah port, this main port serving northern Yemen. As of right now, ships are flowing normally through that port, just with monitoring by a UN body and enforcing the arms embargo. But I'm worried about that being constricted at a time when the US and Iran have competing

blockades in the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis have launched their own blockade of Saudi Arabia. It's very much the trend right now. So I can see that happening, and that would lead to further escalation, certainly, from the Houthis targeting, perhaps, Saudi port infrastructure, oil export infrastructure itself in exchange. And then I'm worried about the battlefield inside of Yemen, because this is ultimately about control inside of Yemen. We've seen Taz, the third largest city in Yemen, be encircled. I'm afraid of what will happen there.

So I think there's still the potential for strategic Houthi gains on the battlefield that will just shift things even deeper. So then talking about the Houthis, what is the biggest thing that Western coverage consistently misses about the Houthis, Alison? We hit on it before, this kind of proxy narrative, this idea of Iranian-backed Houthis, where ultimately, I think it just leads to a reductive view of them that misunderstands both what the group wants, who they are, and how to effectively counter them.

Michael, is that what you think people get most wrong as well? Yeah, and I also think the Houthis are not just an insurgency with national aspirations and a veneer of rational thinking. They are highly ideological with ambitions that defy the imagination. So what I think a lot of observers miss is that this is not just about a threat to Saudi or a threat to oil. This is a threat to commercial traffic to the Red Sea, the stability of countries that border the Red Sea. This is a problem that affects a lot more than Saudi Arabia.

And if I could add one more, maybe. Sure, sure. Neglecting the agency of Yemenis, you know, so many people who view this primarily as a Saudi conflict just focus on Riyadh, and I think what that does is take the Yemen picture out of this. And the framing of this episode has probably furthered that by saying, what options does Saudi Arabia have, not what options do Yemenis have? So I apologise. But OK, finally, then, so we've said a lot of, you know, I think you're not very optimistic

going forward, but it seems you're both expecting more of an escalation. But what's one development that would actually make you optimistic when it comes to this conflict? Michael, can I start with you? Well, here I'm going to sound rather bellicose, but the one thing that would make me optimistic is if the Saudis, we, somebody could just get rid of the Houthi leadership once and for all. OK. Alison? Quite different than Michael, I am looking for either the Houthis or Iran to extend some

sort of fig leaf. I know it sounds crazy to a lot of people, but the Houthis have done this before. In September 2019, they announced a unilateral ceasefire with Saudi Arabia that kicked off, you know, an attempt at de-escalation. Then we did see them release one UN staff member. I'm not sure if that means anything deeper. And then from an Iran, again, they can't control this conflict, but they can help contain it. You know, if Iran were to demonstrate that it's not going to encourage the Iraqi militias to gang up on this fight against the Saudis with the Houthis, that can at least help mitigate

the consequences of the Yemen conflict for the broader Iran crisis. OK. So I think you've described that Saudis have a terrible dilemma. They need to respond to these attacks, but they know that the Houthis can respond asymmetrically and the Houthis have shown that they are prepared to target explicitly civilian targets. There are real challenges among the anti-Houthi coalition as well.

But one of the other problems the Saudis have is that they have experienced this before. They had a very difficult time with their campaign against the Houthis. And so, Alison, I think you said you would really like to see the Saudis articulate credible military goals from this military operation. It does seem ultimately, though, like you're both expecting a Saudi response and that in the short term there will be an escalation and that that probably looks like expanding

the air campaign. We then talked a bit about the U.S. role and, Michael, you said, you know, ultimately we're in a period of highly personalized decision making when it comes to the U.S. involvement in the war. There potentially are military constraints on the U.S. side, but there are also political factors. President Trump wants this war to be over. And Alison, I think you said he tends to like to support sort of winners and he knows that the Saudis have huge challenges when it comes to this campaign.

So I think big questions about exactly what role the U.S. might play. When we talked about the potential for a deal, I think you both think it's unlikely in the short term. Michael, you said it would take a long time and it would take patience to sort of begin to build that political alternative to the Houthis to try to bring together this coalition of anti-Houthi actors in Yemen. And it's hard to talk about a deal when we're currently in an escalatory cycle.

But Alison, you said ultimately we need to be looking for an off-ramp as soon as possible because of the challenges of the military campaign. So Saudi Arabia doesn't have any good choices. I think it's going to be really difficult. But I think, Michael, you shared some of what you heard about Saudis being really quite united at the moment, a sense of solidarity and a sense that this threat really does need to be dealt with because the Houthis have real ambitions and very alarming ambitions.

And so they can't continue to be appeased, perhaps. So I think we're talking on Friday the 16th. This is a really dynamic moment. I think probably some scary times ahead or some worrying times for those in the region. But I think you've really helped us understand how we got here, the options that lay ahead of us, and then some of the pathway of how we might get out of this. So thank you so, so much, Michael and Alison, for your time.

It is an absolute pleasure to have you as colleagues and to have you on the show with me today. I'm really grateful for your time and your insights. Thank you. Anytime. Thanks so much.
